A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EcoLoRA research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: v1 reports original question-answering and value-alignment experiments, network simulations, component ablations, and task-heterogeneity results in Section 4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments varying client counts, participation, local updates, LoRA rank, and asynchronous client selection.

M1.justification: The round-robin segmentation, staleness-weighted model mixing, adaptive sparsification, residual accumulation, and Golomb encoding remain unchanged. Asynchronous participation is introduced as an evaluation setting without a documented revision to EcoLoRA's components.

E1.justification: The datasets and QA/value-alignment tasks remain unchanged. Appendix C adds an operating scenario with asynchronous clients updating at different speeds, extending the tested environment beyond the original participation setting.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain FedIT, FLoRA, FFA-LoRA, federated DPO, and fixed top-k sparsification. New experiments reuse existing comparators; FedBuff supplies the asynchronous aggregation setting rather than appearing as a separately evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Tables 6–10 add protocols using 200/300 total clients, 30/50 participants per round, 3/5 local updates, QA LoRA ranks 8/32, and buffered asynchronous aggregation. These substantially broaden the experimental settings while retaining the original default configuration.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to client population, participation rate, local computation, LoRA rank, and asynchronous selection. Existing component, compression, and task-heterogeneity analyses remain; the fixed top-k comparison is relocated from Appendix C to Section 4.4 rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions' Appendix A states that communication-time experiments are repeated five times and averaged. No additional seed information, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 6–10 add results across the new settings. For example, with 200 clients, FedIT and EcoLoRA both score 66.5 ARC while total communication is 7633.6M versus 2968.2M parameters. Section 4.3 also newly reports 0.89 Mbps throughput at 1 Mbps bandwidth. Original Tables 1–5 and v1 Table 6, now Table 11, retain their values.

T1.justification: Section 3.7 retains the same assumptions, constants, learning-rate conditions, and claimed convergence rate. Appendix B preserves the mathematical derivation; equation rewrapping and reordered explanatory text do not change the theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same methodological contributions, convergence claim, and communication-efficiency claims, including reductions of up to 79% in communication time and 65% in training time.

C2.justification: The limitations section replaces the single-FL-setting and restricted-model-family caveats with a LoRA-only applicability limitation and a proposed modularity-based extension to adapters and prefix tuning. Additional experiments partly address the setting caveat, but model coverage remains restricted despite removal of that explicit qualification.

D1.justification: Section 4.3 newly specifies ns-3 point-to-point TCP communication configured to match standard Linux implementations. Conversely, v1's promise to release code upon publication is removed without replacement access information. Appendix A's preprocessing, hardware, and default hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds contextual citations on privacy and federated fine-tuning, plus FedBuff and Linux TCP references supporting the experimental descriptions. It removes the Mao et al. LoRA-survey reference and substitutes Liu et al. 2024a in the introduction. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 moves the discussion of conventional FL techniques' limitations from Section 3.2 to Section 2.3 and moves the top-k discussion into the main text. It also makes localized wording and terminology edits, expands the encoding explanation, and adds acknowledgments without extensively rewriting the document.

P2.justification: New Tables 6–10 substantially expand the displayed evidence for scaling, participation, local updates, rank, and asynchronous selection. Table 5 moves from the appendix into the main text, and the task-heterogeneity table becomes Table 11. Existing figures retain their content with size and placement adjustments.

improvement.justification: The new sensitivity and asynchronous-participation experiments partly address v1's acknowledged reliance on one FL configuration, strengthening empirical support for applicability. Simulation details also improve documentation. These gains are limited by sparse specification of the asynchronous setup and unchanged accuracy-uncertainty reporting, and are partly offset by removal of code-release information and the still-relevant model-coverage caveat.
